title: The Ventricular Zone: Radial Glia as Stem Cells

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: What two properties define a stem cell?
cards.back: Self-renewal and the ability to make more than one kind of cell.
cards.quote: A stem cell renews itself and can make more than one kind of cell.

cards.front: In the embryonic cortical wall, which surface is apical and which is basal?
cards.back: Apical faces the ventricle; basal faces the basement membrane and pia at the outer surface.
cards.quote: The surface of the wall that faces the ventricle is apical.

cards.front: Why does making neurons in a dish establish a progenitor’s potential rather than its fate in the embryo?
cards.back: The dish shows what it can make under culture conditions. Its fate is what its descendants actually become in the embryo.
cards.quote: A dish tests potential; only lineage in the animal shows fate.

cards.front: How does the number of radial glial daughters retained in a division determine whether that radial glial line grows, persists or ends?
cards.back: Retaining two doubles the line; retaining one preserves it while producing a different daughter; retaining none ends it.
cards.quote: Keep two, and its radial glial line doubles. Keep one, and the line holds steady while it makes neurons.

cards.front: An outer radial glial cell has no apical contact but repeatedly renews itself. Does lack of contact alone exclude stem-cell status, and why?
cards.back: No. Outer radial glia renew without apical contact; contact marks the apical radial glial state, not the definition of a stem cell.
cards.quote: Outer radial glia, rare in mouse and common in primates, renew themselves without any apical contact.

cards.front: A single epithelial cell layer with nuclei at different heights is a {{c1::pseudostratified epithelium}}.
cards.quote: A single layer of cells whose nuclei sit at many heights is called a pseudostratified epithelium.
cards.section: The lift: a nucleus on a timetable

cards.front: In interkinetic nuclear migration in embryonic cortex, trace the nucleus through G1, S, G2 and mitosis.
cards.back: G1: moves basally within the VZ. S: near the basal edge of the VZ. G2: returns apically. Mitosis: at the ventricular surface.
cards.quote: In G2 it comes back down to the ground floor, the apical surface, and the cell divides there.
cards.section: The lift: a nucleus on a timetable

cards.front: A brief DNA-synthesis tracer pulse labels only S-phase nuclei in an embryonic neural wall. Why should labeled mitoses appear later rather than immediately?
cards.back: Labeled cells must finish S phase and pass through G2 before mitosis. Initially labeled nuclei lie farther out in the VZ; later they divide apically.
cards.quote: Soon after the pulse, the labeled nuclei sit out in the VZ, where S phase happens, and no cell in mitosis is labeled.
cards.section: The lift: a nucleus on a timetable

cards.front: In eleven-day mouse embryos, the first thymidine-labeled mitotic figures appeared about an hour after injection. Which cell-cycle interval does this lag roughly estimate, and why?
cards.back: Roughly G2: cells labeled at the end of S phase still had to traverse G2, including movement toward the ventricle, before dividing.
cards.quote: That lag is roughly G2: the cells labeled last in S phase had to pass through G2,
cards.section: The lift: a nucleus on a timetable

cards.front: How does centrosome position help explain apical mitosis in vertebrate neuroepithelia, and what qualification comes from live imaging?
cards.back: The nucleus approaches centrosomes usually positioned apically. In late G2, the centrosome can move toward it, allowing mitosis just short of the surface.
cards.quote: late in G2 the centrosome can leave the surface to meet the incoming nucleus,

cards.front: In an illustrative packing model, mitosis lasts 0.5 hours of a 12-hour cycle. Cells are uniformly distributed through the cycle; mitotic cells occupy 80 µm² apically and others 4 µm². What is the mean apical area per cell?
cards.back: Mitotic fraction = 0.5/12 = 1/24. Mean area = (80 + 23 × 4)/24 = 7.17 µm² per cell, about 7 µm².
cards.quote: Staggered timetables let more progenitors share a given area of ventricle.

cards.front: Why is mitosis at the ventricular surface a clue, rather than proof, that a cortical progenitor is an apical radial glial cell?
cards.back: Some intermediate progenitors also divide there. Add shape and markers to identify the cell; lineage is needed to learn its daughters’ fates.
cards.quote: Most mitoses at the ventricle are apical radial glia (or, earlier, neuroepithelial cells), though some intermediate progenitors divide there too.

cards.front: A micrograph shows young neurons touching radial glial fibres. Why does this observation alone fail to establish that radial glia produced those neurons?
cards.back: Contact supports a scaffold role but does not reveal ancestry. Following the descendants of an identified radial glial cell would test neuronal origin.
cards.quote: To learn what its daughters become, you need lineage, the descendants of one cell.

cards.front: How did a human GFAP-promoter GFP reporter allow embryonic mouse radial glia to be sorted for tests of neuronal potential despite their low endogenous GFAP protein?
cards.back: The human promoter fragment was active in radial glia, making them GFP-positive. Reporter activity did not require abundant endogenous mouse GFAP protein.
cards.quote: Embryonic rodent radial glia make little GFAP protein of their own, but this fragment of the human promoter is active in them.

cards.front: Why can a mouse neuron retain a Cre-activated lineage reporter after the GFAP promoter has switched off?
cards.back: Cre removes a DNA stop sequence. Descendants inherit that permanent change, so reporter labeling records ancestry rather than current GFAP-promoter activity.
cards.quote: The cut is a change in the DNA, so it is copied into every descendant,

cards.front: A rat cortical-slice film follows an identified radial glial cell through division and shows one daughter becoming a neuron. Which hypothesis does this directly contradict, and why?
cards.back: A scaffold-only role: directly following a radial glial cell into a neuronal daughter demonstrates neuronal ancestry, not merely contact with a fibre.
cards.quote: The dish and the recordings made it unlikely; the fate map and the films showed neuronal ancestry directly.

cards.front: Rat cortical precursors recorded with an electrode are dye-filled and found to have radial glial shape. Why does this identify the sampled cells without proving their neuronal descendants?
cards.back: Dye filling reveals the sampled cells’ morphology. It does not follow their daughters, and electrode access limits which cells are sampled.
cards.quote: recorded from precursors with an electrode, then filled each recorded cell with dye.

cards.front: How do an animal fate map and a live cortical-slice lineage film strengthen the case for radial glial neuronal ancestry when considered together?
cards.back: The animal map establishes ancestry in vivo but depends on promoter timing. The film follows an identified cell’s daughters directly but only in a slice for hours to days. The rule is convergence across methods with different blind spots.
cards.quote: Each has a blind spot, but the blind spots differ, so together they persuaded.

cards.front: What daughters does an asymmetric radial glial division produce in direct neurogenesis?
cards.back: One radial glial cell and one neuron.
cards.quote: In direct neurogenesis, a radial glial cell divides into another radial glial cell and a neuron.

cards.front: In indirect cortical neurogenesis, a radial glial cell produces another radial glial cell and an {{c1::intermediate progenitor}}.
cards.back: In rodent cortex, that progenitor usually divides once more into two neurons.
cards.quote: In indirect neurogenesis, the second daughter is an intermediate progenitor.

cards.front: In the mouse cortical lineage, which transcription-factor markers correspond to radial glia, intermediate progenitors and neurons?
cards.back: Pax6 → radial glia; Tbr2 (Eomes) → intermediate progenitors; Tbr1 → neurons.
cards.quote: radial glia (Pax6) → intermediate progenitor (Tbr2) → neuron (Tbr1)

cards.front: In the early mouse Tbr2-deletion models, apical divisions continued, divisions away from the ventricle fell and fewer cortical neurons formed. Which neurogenic route was impaired?
cards.back: The indirect route. Reduced divisions away from the ventricle indicate loss of the intermediate-progenitor amplification step; continued apical divisions show that not all neurogenesis stopped.
cards.quote: In those mutants Tbr2 was needed for the indirect route, not for all neurogenesis.

cards.front: A later mouse Tbr2-deletion model shows more divisions away from the ventricle but failed neuronal differentiation. Why would counting basal mitoses alone misjudge neuron production?
cards.back: A dividing intermediate progenitor has not yet become a neuron. The counting rule distinguishes division from neuronal exit; the later deletion model shows that more basal divisions need not yield more neurons.
cards.quote: in a later one, divisions away from the ventricle rose and the intermediate progenitors failed to become neurons

cards.front: The local setting that maintains a stem cell’s stem state is its {{c1::niche}}.
cards.quote: A niche is the local setting that keeps a stem cell a stem cell.
cards.section: What a leaving daughter gives up

cards.front: In embryonic mouse cortex, an asymmetric apical radial glial division produces one radial glial daughter and one neuron. How does their access to the CSF side of the niche differ, and why?
cards.back: The departing daughter loses direct apical contact with the CSF niche; the retained radial glial daughter keeps it. Access follows whether the apical contact is maintained.
cards.quote: The daughter that stays keeps it, and with it the signals that support dividing.
cards.section: What a leaving daughter gives up

cards.front: Why does loss of apical contact not necessarily mean that a cortical progenitor immediately stops dividing?
cards.back: Intermediate progenitors detach yet usually divide again; outer radial glia can self-renew without apical contact. Contact loss and cell-cycle exit are distinct.
cards.quote: an intermediate progenitor has let go and still divides once more, and outer radial glia renew themselves without it.
cards.section: What a leaving daughter gives up

cards.front: In a model where every progenitor divides once and daughters either remain progenitors or become neurons, the fractions P (stay) and Q (quit) obey {{c1::P + Q = 1}}.
cards.quote: Call P the fraction of daughters that stay progenitors and Q the fraction that quit the cycle as neurons, so P + Q = 1.

cards.front: In a no-death model, every progenitor divides once per round and daughters either stay progenitors or become neurons. If Q, the fraction becoming neurons, stays at 0.5, what happens to the dividing pool and why?
cards.back: It stays constant while producing neurons. Each N-cell pool makes 2N daughters: N stay progenitors and N become neurons.
cards.quote: 2N daughters, half staying, gives N progenitors again, plus N neurons.

cards.front: A closed pool starts with 200 progenitors. Each divides once per round; daughters either keep dividing or become neurons. Q is 0.25 in round one and 0.75 in round two. How many neurons form in total, and how many progenitors remain?
cards.back: Round 1: 400 daughters → 100 neurons + 300 progenitors. Round 2: 600 daughters → 450 neurons + 150 progenitors. Total: 550 neurons; 150 progenitors remain.
cards.quote: next pool = 2N × P; neurons made this round = 2N × Q

cards.front: In a closed progenitor-pool model, Q is the fraction of all daughters becoming neurons. A researcher measures Q = 0.5 and concludes every division was asymmetric. Why is that conclusion unjustified?
cards.back: Q describes daughters across the pool, not individual divisions. Equal numbers of two-progenitor and two-neuron divisions also give Q = 0.5. By the pool-counting rule, daughter totals do not uniquely identify division modes.
cards.quote: Call P the fraction of daughters that stay progenitors and Q the fraction that quit the cycle as neurons,

cards.front: Why must radial glia and intermediate progenitors be counted separately when estimating the self-renewing cortical stem pool?
cards.back: Both divide, but intermediate progenitors usually divide only once more. A larger combined dividing pool can therefore conceal an unchanged radial glial stem pool.
cards.quote: The pool is every dividing cell, so 2N × P is not a count of stem cells

cards.front: One radial glial cell makes one radial glial cell and one intermediate progenitor per round. Each intermediate progenitor divides into two neurons in the next round. Starting with no intermediate progenitors, what cells are present immediately after round five?
cards.back: Radial glia = 1. Four earlier intermediate progenitors have each made 2 neurons: 4 × 2 = 8 neurons. The fifth intermediate progenitor remains: 1 intermediate progenitor.
cards.quote: intermediate progenitors multiply, and delay, what each spent daughter yields.

cards.front: Why can a progenitor pool that initially keeps most daughters dividing later produce more neurons than one that immediately spends many daughters?
cards.back: Early retention expands the pool. Later divisions then start with more progenitors, increasing neuronal output when more daughters exit, under the closed-pool counting model.
cards.quote: In the first five cycles almost nothing is made and the pool multiplies.

cards.front: How does the cell cycle change across neurogenesis in mouse dorsal cortex?
cards.back: It lengthens from about 8 hours at embryonic day 11 to about 18 hours near the end; nearly all added time is G1.
cards.quote: In mouse dorsal cortex it lengthens from about 8 hours at embryonic day 11 to about 18 hours near the end of neurogenesis,

cards.front: A drug lengthens G1 without arresting the cycle in embryonic cortical progenitors. What daughter-level measurement would test whether it raises Q, rather than merely slowing divisions?
cards.back: Follow completed divisions and measure the fraction of daughters becoming neurons versus continuing to divide, compared with controls. The rule is that Q measures daughter outcomes per division, whereas cycle duration measures time.
cards.quote: a drug that lengthened G1 without stopping the cycle led to early neurogenesis in the forebrain neuroepithelium

cards.front: Two identical progenitor pools have the same daughter fates per division, but one has a longer cell cycle. Within a fixed developmental interval, what happens to its number of completed rounds, and why?
cards.back: It completes fewer rounds because each takes longer. Matching daughter fates per division does not compensate for fewer opportunities to divide.
cards.quote: In mouse dorsal cortex it lengthens from about 8 hours at embryonic day 11 to about 18 hours near the end of neurogenesis,

cards.front: One radial glial cell undergoes five divisions, retaining one radial glial daughter each time. Compare final neuron yield for direct output versus one intermediate progenitor per division, each later making two neurons. Wait until all intermediate progenitors have divided.
cards.back: Direct: 5 × 1 = 5 neurons. Indirect: 5 × 2 = 10 neurons. One radial glial cell remains in either case.
cards.quote: Routing output through intermediate progenitors doubles the neurons per radial glial division without spending the radial glial cell.

cards.front: One radial glial founder first makes two radial glia. Each then undergoes four self-renewing divisions, each producing an intermediate progenitor that later makes two neurons. After all intermediate progenitors divide, how does output compare with omitting the initial expansion?
cards.back: With expansion: 2 × 4 × 2 = 16 neurons and 2 radial glia. Without it: 1 × 4 × 2 = 8 neurons and 1 radial glial cell. Rule: early stem-pool doubling doubles later output for an identical subsequent division schedule.
cards.quote: A symmetric proliferative division, radial glia into two radial glia, makes no neurons now but doubles every later output.

cards.front: A verified single neural progenitor makes neurons and non-neuronal cells in culture. Why does this alone fail to establish that it was a self-renewing stem cell in the embryo?
cards.back: The clone establishes multiple-cell-type potential in culture. Stem-cell status also requires self-renewal, and embryonic fate requires animal lineage evidence. Those are separate requirements in the stem-cell definition and potential-versus-fate rule.
cards.quote: A well shows potential, not fate, and her cells came from the forebrain as a whole,
cards.section: The clonal study: potential, not fate

cards.front: Why can a lineage reporter driven by a late-activating promoter underestimate a progenitor population’s neuronal contribution?
cards.back: Neurons produced before promoter activation will not inherit the mark. An unlabeled neuron can therefore reflect late labeling rather than ancestry from another progenitor population.
cards.quote: A fate map is only as early as the promoter that drives it.
cards.section: When the GFAP promoter switches on

cards.front: Why is roughly eight or nine neurons per neurogenic mouse radial glial cell not directly comparable to about 150 neurons in the illustrative founder model?
cards.back: The model lets a founder first expand its dividing pool. The lineage estimate is per radial glial cell after it starts making neurons: different denominators.
cards.quote: the MADM figure is per radial glial cell once it has turned to making neurons.
cards.section: How many neurons per radial glial cell?
